---
title: "Behavioral policy optimization"
---

Behavioral policy optimization (BPO) changes how an agent collects data, not
which gradient it wants to estimate. In trajectory-based BPO [@papini2024],
one draw is a complete trajectory. More generally, one draw can be any variable
$X$ whose probability mass or density we can evaluate and from which we compute
a gradient contribution $g(X)$.

## What counts as one draw?

Let $p(x)$ be the fixed reference distribution and
$\mu=\mathbb E_p[g(X)]$ the gradient we want to estimate. Write $q_\beta(x)$
for the distribution of $X$ induced by the behavioral policy $\beta$ and the
**sampling protocol**: how a run starts, when it is observed or stopped, and
what is recorded as one draw.

- For an immediate sensory observation recorded at stationarity, $q_\beta$ is
  the stationary distribution of observations under $\beta$. Recording the
  observation just after reset generally gives a different distribution.
- For trajectory-based BPO, set $X=\tau$. Then $p(\tau)$ and $q_\beta(\tau)$
  are the trajectory distributions under the target and behavioral policies,
  respectively, given the initial-state distribution and stopping rule. No
  stationarity assumption is needed.

## Which draws reduce variance?

If we sample $X$ from a proposal $q$ instead of $p$, the importance-weighted
estimate is $Y=p(X)g(X)/q(X)$. Its expectation is still $\mu$, provided $q$
is positive wherever $p(x)\|g(x)\|_2$ is positive. To minimize the sum of the
component variances of $Y$, it suffices to minimize its second moment:
$\mathbb E_q[\|Y\|_2^2]$, since $\|\mu\|_2^2$ is fixed. By Cauchy–Schwarz,
this second moment is at least $(\mathbb E_q[\|Y\|_2])^2$, with equality when
the weighted estimate has constant norm. The proposal that achieves this is
$$
q^*(x)=\frac{p(x)\|g(x)\|_2}{\mathbb E_p[\|g(X)\|_2]},
$$
assuming the denominator is finite and nonzero. Relative to the reference
distribution, this proposal samples inputs with large gradient contributions
more often and compensates by giving each such draw less weight.

This result treats $g(x)$ as fixed once $x$ is known. If the contribution $G$
is still random given $X$, and changing the policy leaves its conditional law
given $X$ unchanged, the optimal factor in place of $\|g(x)\|_2$ is
$\sqrt{\mathbb E[\|G\|_2^2\mid X=x]}$.

## Fitting the behavioral policy

Fit $q_\beta$ to the optimal proposal by minimizing the cross-entropy **from
$q^*$ to $q_\beta$**, namely $-\mathbb E_{q^*}[\log q_\beta(X)]$.
For reference observations $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ sampled from $p$, the resulting
empirical objective, up to a positive factor independent of $\beta$, is
$$
\underset{\beta}{\operatorname{minimize}}\quad
-\sum_{i=1}^n \|g(x_i)\|_2\,\log q_\beta(x_i).
$$
The sample frequencies supply the empirical distribution of $X$; each draw's
gradient norm supplies its additional weight. If the policy family can realize
$q^*$, minimizing the population cross-entropy recovers the single-draw
optimum. Otherwise it finds the closest realizable proposal in forward KL
divergence, $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q^*\|q_\beta)$, which need not be the policy with
the lowest variance.

The variance above is for **one draw**, without conditioning on the history
that led to it. The same proposal is optimal for an average of independent,
identically distributed draws, whose variance is the single-draw variance
divided by the number of draws. For consecutive observations at stationarity,
the variance of the average also depends on temporal covariances. With correct
importance weights, correlation does not bias a fixed-length average, but
matching the stationary distribution alone need not minimize its variance.
